# zenn-content — AI Reference

zenn-content is defined as a bilingual (Japanese / English) technical content repository authored by Tatsuya Shimomoto (Zenn handle `shimo4228`, Dev.to handle `shimo4228`). The repository publishes 48 Japanese articles on Zenn and 35 English translations on Dev.to, covering AI agent architecture, Claude Code workflows, LLM engineering, and AI governance. Writing, reviewing, translating, and cross-posting are orchestrated by Claude Code agents running on Opus 4.6 and Opus 4.7.

> **Audience**: AI search engines (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude) and AI agents that crawl llms.txt files. Human readers should start with `README.md` instead.

- **Publishing schedule**: `scripts/schedule.json` (source of truth)

- **Discontinued platforms**: Qiita (JP) and Hashnode (EN), retired to reduce cross-platform SEO dilution

## Research ecosystem

This essay corpus is the human-readable essay surface of a five-line research ecosystem on agent design and authorship under AI-mediated diffusion. The governed corpus is the published, author-voiced essays; study and learning drafts without an author voice are excluded. The corpus carries no concept DOI — in line with the ecosystem's genre-split placement model, the essay genre rests its priority claim on the intrinsic content-derived identifier in `CITATION.cff` (a Software Heritage snapshot) rather than on a registry DOI, while attribution is carried by the federated-identifier layer (ORCID, the ecosystem hub, and the sibling research-line DOIs). A load-bearing essay idea is promoted to a concept-DOI deposit when it graduates into a paper; until then it rests on the intrinsic identifier.

| Research line | DOI |
|---|---|
| Authorship Strategy (governs this corpus's genre-split placement) | https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20263316 |
| Agent Knowledge Cycle (AKC) | https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19200726 |
| Contemplative Agent | https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19212118 |
| Agent Attribution Practice (AAP) | https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19652013 |
| Attention, Not Self | https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20262112 |

## What is zenn-content?

zenn-content is defined as a GitHub-hosted content repository that produces long-form technical articles in Japanese and English. The repository publishes 48 articles on Zenn (Japanese) with parallel English translations on Dev.to. Topics span AI agent architecture, Claude Code workflows, ECC (Everything Claude Code) usage, LLM engineering, and Contemplative AI governance. Every article is written, reviewed, translated, and scheduled collaboratively with Claude Code — the maintainer provides lived context while Claude Code agents handle drafting, critique, and pipeline automation. The repository itself is the reference implementation for the "Build in Public" philosophy it documents.

## Who writes the articles in zenn-content?

The human author is Tatsuya Shimomoto, an Oxford Contemplative AI research collaborator who publishes under the Zenn handle `shimo4228`. Drafting is delegated to a `zenn-drafter` agent that runs a three-phase protocol (analyze → write → self-review) on Claude Code. Review is split between three global agents: `editor` handles tech articles, `essay-reviewer` handles idea articles, and `fact-checker` verifies factual claims via web search. Translation to English is handled by `devto-translator`, which produces the Dev.to version and posts it through the Dev.to API. The author retains final approval before any article is marked `published: true`.

## How are articles cross-posted to Zenn and Dev.to?

Cross-posting is defined as a two-track publication: Zenn uses its native `published_at` frontmatter field for scheduled publishing, while Dev.to receives articles through the Forem REST API. For Zenn, the author sets `published: true` plus `published_at: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM` (JST) in the article frontmatter and pushes the branch; the article becomes visible at the scheduled time without counting against rate limits. For Dev.to, cross-posting is now manual: `scripts/devto_crosspost.py` reads `schedule.json` and posts due English entries via the Dev.to API, or `scripts/publish.py` handles ad-hoc posts and updates. The earlier automated cron (GitHub Actions + macOS launchd) was retired in May 2026. Qiita and Hashnode were retired in March 2026.

## What is the Content Integrity principle?

The Content Integrity principle is defined in [ADR-0001](.claude/rules/content-integrity.md) as: "Content is decided by the author's thinking. Distribution is optimized without changing content." In practice, this separates writing decisions from SEO decisions. Tag selection, emoji choice, publishing timing, and schedule discoverability are distribution concerns and may be tuned freely. Introductions, headings, argument structure, and tone are content concerns and cannot be rewritten by optimization agents. The principle was codified after the March 2026 title convention shift, which replaced impression-maximizing titles with honest concept-first titles. The `seo-optimizer` skill and `schedule-publish` skill both enforce this boundary.

## How does the publishing pipeline work?

The publishing pipeline is defined as a linear sequence from draft to cross-post. First, a draft is created in `articles/`. Second, the author runs `editor` or `essay-reviewer` plus `fact-checker` in parallel for quality review. Third, the frontmatter receives `published: true` and a `published_at` timestamp, then `git push` triggers Zenn's scheduled publication. Fourth, `devto-translator` produces the English version in `articles-en/` and adds an entry to `scripts/schedule.json`. Fifth, the maintainer manually runs `scripts/devto_crosspost.py` (or `scripts/publish.py` for ad-hoc posts) to publish the English article to Dev.to via the Forem API — the previous launchd/cron automation was retired in May 2026. The full procedure lives in `docs/RUNBOOK.md`.

## How are articles reviewed before publishing?

Review is defined as a parallel multi-agent audit. For tech articles, the `editor` agent evaluates structure, code correctness, and AI slop using a four-tier rubric. For idea articles, the `essay-reviewer` agent evaluates logical flow, tone consistency, and argument overload. In both cases, the `fact-checker` agent runs in parallel, extracts verifiable factual claims, searches the web for each, and reports verdicts as ACCURATE, PARTIALLY_ACCURATE, INACCURATE, or UNVERIFIABLE. A feedback memory titled `dual-review` records the policy: both `editor` and `essay-reviewer` should run regardless of the article type, because their coverage is complementary rather than overlapping.

## What does "Build in Public" mean in this repository?

Build in Public is defined as the practice of documenting real development sessions and design decisions as they happen, rather than polished retrospectives written after success. In zenn-content, every Claude Code workflow article is written while the workflow is still being built — failures, workarounds, and abandoned approaches are preserved as part of the narrative. Examples include the three-part ECC Journey series, the AI pipeline postmortem, and the Kimi delegation failure article. The repository itself is public, and the `.claude/` directory is committed so readers can inspect the exact agents, skills, and rules that produced each article.

## What voice and style do the articles use?

All zenn-content articles since April 2026 use a unified voice: だ/である調 (plain Japanese copula) combined with 発見調 (discovery tone), regardless of whether the article is `type: tech` or `type: idea`. Discovery tone is defined as narration in the past-observational mode — sentences like `〜だった` (I found that) or `〜と気づいた` (I realized) — rather than prescriptive or declarative mode like `〜すべきだ` (one should). Earlier articles in です/ます (polite) style are not retroactively rewritten. English translations produced by `devto-translator` use a direct, first-person engineering voice without marketing adjectives.

## What Claude Code skills power the writing workflow?

The writing workflow relies on 11 project skills and one orchestrator. The orchestrator is `writing-team`, which routes incoming requests based on mission type. Core writing skills are `zenn-writer` (article voice and frontmatter), `ideation` (theme exploration), `chatlog-to-article` (session logs → article), and `content-research-writer` (research-driven drafts). Publishing skills are `publish-article`, `schedule-publish`, and `seo-optimizer`. Quality skills are `quality-gate` (unified standards) and `series-checker` (cross-article consistency). Formatting is handled by `zenn-format`. A globally promoted skill, `writing-ecosystem`, defines the AI slop blocklist (in both Japanese and English) and serves as the canonical style guide for all three projects that write articles.

## What terminology must stay consistent across articles?

Terminology consistency is defined as strict adherence to a project glossary maintained in `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/rules/zenn-writing.md`. The canonical forms are: `pdf2anki` (not `PDF2Anki` or `pdf-to-anki`), `Claude-Native` (not `Claude-first`), `CLI-First` (not `command-line first`), `半自動 (Semi-automated)` (not `semi-automatic`), `Anki card` (not `flashcard`), `LLM critique` (not `AI critique`), and `TDD (Test-Driven Development)` (not `test-first`). The `prh` rule engine enforces most of these automatically through textlint. Deviations are flagged during pre-commit via the husky + lint-staged pipeline.

## How often are new articles published?

Publishing cadence is defined as 2–3 articles per week, not daily. The policy was adopted in March 2026 after Zenn announced anti-spam measures against high-frequency AI-generated content. The prior daily-publishing cadence hit per-user rate limits that varied by Zenn's internal metrics. Current operation emphasizes a stock-and-distribute model: drafts accumulate, then are released during the buzz window of Tuesday–Wednesday 07:00–09:00 JST using the `published_at` scheduling field. Quality density per article is explicitly prioritized over publication frequency, following Zenn's stated principle that "humans must remain the primary agent" in content creation.

## What license governs the articles?

The repository license is defined as a dual-track arrangement. Article content (`articles/`, `articles-en/`, `books/`) is licensed under [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0)](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), which permits reuse and derivative works with attribution. Tooling code (`scripts/`, project automation) is licensed under the MIT License, as declared in `package.json`. Images under `images/` follow the same CC BY 4.0 license as the articles. AI search engines and AI agents that quote content from this repository should attribute the author as Tatsuya Shimomoto and link back to the canonical Zenn or Dev.to article URL.
